list.listitem: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) comprises a heterogeneous group of precancerous breast lesions, each having a somewhat different prognosis and management strategy. Because of this heterogeneity and because 80% of the lesions are nonpalpable, the diagnosis and treatment of DCIS is complex. C
DCIS is usually suspected based on microcalcifications identified during mammography and confirmed with ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy. B

Treatment options include mastectomy or lumpectomy with subsequent radiation therapy (with or without tamoxifen). Mortality rates between the 2 therapies are likely similar despite increased local and regional recurrence with lumpectomy. B
For women with hormone-receptor positive DCIS, treatment with either tamoxifen or anastrozole may result in fewer recurrences. B

background.definition: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) comprises a heterogeneous group of precancerous breast lesions, each having a somewhat different prognosis and management strategy. DCIS can progress to invasive cancer but estimates of that likelihood vary widely. In the National Institutes of Health (NIH) consensus statement, DCIS is defined as spectrum of abnormal cells confined to the breast duct and is a risk factor for invasive breast cancer development.

list.listitem: The frequency of diagnosis of DCIS has increased markedly in the United States because of widespread use of screening mammography. In 1998, DCIS accounted for approximately 18% (15%-25%) of all newly-diagnosed invasive and non-invasive breast tumors.

Based on data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results registry 2000-2014, there were 145,670 women diagnosed with DCIS with a range of 32,145 cases in 2012-2014 to 41,783 in 2008-2011. The majority (77.8%) of cases were among whites, for whom rates were stable over this time period. Among Black women, making up 10.8% of total cases, and women of other races, incidence increased by 1.6% annually. Similarly, incidence rates increased among younger women (1.3% for women age 20-44 years, and 0.6% for those aged 45-55 years).
In 1 study of mammography in a population of more than 49,000 women, DCIS was detected in 0.2% (103/42,760); invasive carcinoma was detected in 0.5%.

The average age-adjusted incidence of DCIS among women older than 40 years in California was 45.3/100,000 in white women, 35.0/100,000 in black women, 30.9/100,000 in Asian/Pacific Islander women, and 21.8/100,000 in Hispanic women. The NIH consensus statement (2009) reported the current age-adjusted incidence rate of DCIS as 32.5 per 100,000 women; at ages 50 to 64 years, the incidence is approximately 88 per 100,000.

In the Florida Cancer Data System, 23,810 patients with DCIS were identified from 1981 to 2001. The median age was 64 years; 85% were white, 6.6% were African American, and 7.5% were Hispanic. Of those receiving surgical treatment (8% did not), 53% underwent mastectomy and the remainder had breast-conserving therapy.
As of January 1, 2005, an estimated one-half million US women were living with a diagnosis of DCIS.
See Risk Factors below.
DCIS is pathologically defined by the presence of carcinoma cells in well-defined ductal structures without penetration of the duct wall.

DCIS can be subdivided in different ways from a clinical and pathological perspective including method of detection (palpable [20%] vs. mammographic [80%]); architectural patterns (comedo, papillary, micropapillary, cribriform, and solid); and other features.
Among the architectural patterns, comedo-type DICS appears to be more aggressive with a higher probability of associated invasive ductal carcinoma.
The NIH consensus statement (2009) notes that more than one-half of DCIS cases include at least 2 different histologic types in the same breast.
Cases of mixed ductal/lobular carcinoma appear to have lower metastatic spread rates but higher rates of second primary breast cancers.

The USPSTF recommends screening mammography every 2 years for women age 50 to 75 years. B Women age 40 to 49 should consider biennial mammography based on a shared decision based on their risk of breast cancer and values.C

The USPSTF recommends offering risk-reducing medications (e.g., tamoxifen, raloxifene, or aromatase inhibitors) to women age 35 years and older who are at increased risk for breast cancer and at low risk for adverse medication effects. B
For additional breast cancer screening and prevention information, see Breast Cancer topic.

The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening mammography every 2 years for women age 50 to 75 years. Women age 40 to 49 should consider biennial mammography based on a shared decision based on their risk of breast cancer and values; women with an elevated risk such as due to a first degree relative with breast cancer should strongly consider initiating mammography at age 40.

The American College of Radiology (ACR, 2017) recommends mammography or digital breast tomosynthesis screening for average-risk (i.e., <15% lifetime risk of breast cancer) and intermediate-risk (i.e., personal history of breast cancer, lobular neoplasia, atypical ductal hyperplasia, or 15%-20% lifetime risk of breast cancer) women. Ultrasound may be appropriate for either, and for intermediate-risk women, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without and with contrast may also be appropriate.
Mammography, digital breast tomosynthesis, and MRI without and with contrast are appropriate for screening high risk women, although clinical trials are largely lacking.

The USPSTF recommends offering risk-reducing medications (e.g., tamoxifen, raloxifene, or aromatase inhibitors) to women age 35 years and older who are at increased risk for breast cancer and at low risk for adverse medication effects. B They recommend against the routine use of these medications in women who are not at increased risk for breast cancer.

Authors of a Bayesian network meta-analysis of 9 RCTs found that compared with placebo, use of endocrine therapy in high-risk pre- or post-menopausal women reduced the risk of DCIS (odds ratio [OR] 0.74, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.56-0.98). Treatment also reduced the risk of any breast cancer (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.56-0.85), invasive breast cancer (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.53-0.89), and estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.38-0.64), but increased risk of pulmonary embolism (OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.05-1.69), total venous thrombosis (OR 1.75, 95% CI 1.28-2.38), and endometrial carcinoma (OR 1.84, 95% CI 1.17-2.88).

In a follow-up study of women enrolled in 2 RCTs of 5-year treatment with anastrozole for breast cancer reduction, there was a significant and continued reduction in breast cancers, including reduced risk of DCIS (hazard ratio [HR] 0.41, 95% CI 0.22-0.79), especially in women known to be estrogen receptor-positive (HR 0.22, 0.78-0.65). There was no significant difference in overall deaths observed.
DCIS is usually suspected based on microcalcifications identified during mammography; only 20% of lesions are palpable. C
The diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy, usually ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy. B
The extent of disease can be further delineated by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Well-defined margins, spongy consistency; confirmed by ultrasound
Discrete, well-defined margins, mobile; confirmed by biopsy

list.listitem: The most important features of the history are family history in a first-degree relative and the presence of a breast mass.
Masses that are fixed, have irregular borders, and are hard are more likely to be present with cancer. However, with DCIS, a mass is only found in approximately 20% of patients.

Nipple discharge alone is not usually a sign of breast cancer; in a case series of 86 women undergoing operation for nipple discharge (40% bloody), histopathology in 59 women showed duct ectasia, 25 had benign ductal papilloma, 1 had DCIS, and 1 had lobular carcinoma-in-situ.
The average tumor size of DCIS is approximately 1.0 to 1.5 cm.

Mammography is currently the initial diagnostic modality for screening and diagnosis of breast masses; 80% of cases of DCIS are not palpable and are detected with imaging. See chapter on breast cancer for more on mammography. Using screening and diagnostic mammograms and ultrasound (US) images, radiologists were quite accurate in predicting the presence of invasive cancer (AUC values 0.830-0.907) and DCIS (AUC values 0.731-0.837) in one study.

In a retrospective Chinese study, calcification present on mammography was associated with a high pathologic grade of DCIS (OR 3.2, 95% CI 1.3-7.8): pathologic grade was not associated with calcification morphology or distribution, breast density, age, menopausal status, or mammography BI-RADS.

In a retrospective study of 484 cases of DCIS from an institution transitioning from film to digital mammography between 2001 and 2014, 158 (33%) were detected on film and 326 (67%) were detected on digital mammography. Although the overall detection rate was higher with digital vs. film mammography (1.4 and 0.7 per 1000, respectively) and there was a doubling of detection rate of high-grade DCIS (0.8 and 0.4 per 1000, respectively), similar proportions of high-grade versus low- to intermediate-grade DCIS were detected with both modalities and there was no significant difference in the upgrade rate of DCIS to invasive cancer (10% each).

In the evaluation of abnormal calcifications found on mammography, high-resolution MRI (using a microscopy coil) was an accurate test. Nuclear imaging (scintimammography) can also be considered in diagnosing in situ ductal and lobular breast carcinomas.

Both core-needle biopsy and fine-needle aspiration biopsy have been used to further evaluate questionable lesions found on mammography with similar success rates for palpable lesions. However, for evaluation of calcifications in nonpalpable breast lesions, ultrasound-guided core-biopsy performed better than stereotactic-guided biopsy.

MR mammography appears to have high diagnostic accuracy but is unable to distinguish between invasive lobular and DCIS. The apparent diffusion coefficient in MR diffusion weighted imaging, however, can be useful in differentiating tumor architecture between infiltrating ductal carcinoma and DCIS.

Preoperative MRI in women with DCIS was associated with increased odds of having initial mastectomy but not with improvement in surgical outcomes. In another study, routine use of breast MRI in the diagnostic work-up for 81 women diagnosed with DCIS resulted in identification of occult malignancy in one and 46 additional findings that led to 23 procedures and 16 negative biopsies. Pre-operative MR findings may be helpful in predicting recurrence.

However, authors of a systematic review of 3 RCTs and 23 observational cohorts, including 20,415 patients, found no evidence of a benefit to pre-operative MRI on surgical outcomes for women with DCIS lesions, based on low to very-low certainty evidence. In addition, in an RCT of 360 patients with DCIS, use of pre-operative MRI did not significantly reduce the rate of rehospitalization for positive or close margins (20% vs. 27% in the no-MRI arm); total costs were no different for the two strategies.

Use of dynamic contrast-enhanced MR imaging with computer-aided diagnosis was helpful in one study for identifying an invasive component to DCIS among 138 patients with DCIS who underwent preoperative breast MRI. In this study, multivariate analysis revealed that delay washout on computer aided diagnosis (OR 4.4, 95% CI 2.0-9.7) and pathologic size (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.1-1.6) were independent predictors for presence of an invasive component.

The optimal diagnostic method for evaluation of nipple discharge is unknown. One study found that duct sonography had the highest sensitivity (67%), followed by MRI (65%), galactography (56%), ductoscopy (55%), and fine-needle aspiration cytology (52%); the highest specificity was for fine-needle aspiration cytology, core biopsy, and galactography (each 100%).

Autoantibodies to known tumor-associated proteins might be useful in early diagnosis; one study found at least 1 of 6 antigens present in 64% of women with primary breast cancer and 45% of women with DCIS.

Overinterpretation of breast biopsies is common, so dual reading of all specimens by experienced, high-volume pathologists is important. In one study, 17.4% of DCIS samples were overinterpreted, and the most effective way to reduce this was if all specimens were examined by two pathologists (not only those classified initially as invasive cancer).
DCIS is usually suspected based on microcalcifications identified during mammography; only 20% of lesions are palpable masses.
The diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy, usually ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy.
The extent of disease can be further delineated by MRI, but use of MRI may not improve surgical outcomes.

A multidisciplinary international Expert Panel on behalf of the American Society of Clinical Oncology/College of American Pathologists recommends estrogen receptor (ER) testing of DCIS and invasive breast cancers by validated immunohistochemistry as the standard for predicting which patients may benefit from endocrine therapy; breast cancer samples with 1% to 100% of tumor nuclei positive are interpreted as ER positive.

Mastectomy has been the traditional approach to DCIS; it is considered the treatment of choice for DCIS with microinvasion and/or pleomorphic microcalcifications in more than one quadrant on mammography. A

Localized DCIS is usually treated with lumpectomy and follow-up radiation therapy. Although not specific to DCIS, there are comparable effects on mortality for breast-conserving therapy compared with mastectomy for early breast cancer despite increased local and regional recurrence with lumpectomy. B
Tamoxifen or anastrozole may offer additional benefits to women with ER-positive tumors electing to undergo lumpectomy with or without radiation. B

Tamoxifen may offer additional benefits to women electing to undergo lumpectomy with radiation. In a large RCT, women randomized to receive tamoxifen (20 mg/day for 5 years) versus placebo had significantly fewer breast cancer events (same side and/or opposite side recurrence or metastases) at 5-year follow-up (8.2% vs. 13.4%). The benefit attributable to tamoxifen was confined to ER-positive tumors.

A study reported a median 13.7 years of follow-up of 1701 patients in the NSABP B-17 trial which randomized women with completely locally-excised DCIS to radiotherapy and tamoxifen, radiotherapy alone, tamoxifen alone, or to no adjuvant treatment. The 794 women who received tamoxifen (with or without radiotherapy) had fewer new breast cancers or DCIS compared to 782 women who had no tamoxifen (18.1% vs. 24.6%, p <0.05, NNT = 16). About 60% in both groups had cancer and 40% DCIS. Among 523 patients who received radiotherapy, the addition of tamoxifen conferred no additional benefit (new breast cancer or DCIS 4.1% with tamoxifen vs. 5.6% without tamoxifen).

Mastectomy followed by tamoxifen is the traditional treatment for breast cancers that are estrogen receptor-positive. We were unable to find evidence supporting treatment of DCIS with mastectomy followed by tamoxifen.

Anastrozole, an aromatase inhibitor, appears as effective as tamoxifen with respect to recurrence (4.6% vs. 5.2%, respectively) and death (2.3% vs. 2.4%, respectively), based on the IBIS-II RCT of 2980 postmenopausal women with hormone-positive DCIS treated by lumpectomy, with median follow-up of 7 years. Rates of adverse effects were similar and nearly universal (91% vs. 93%), although side effects differed with more musculoskeletal events (including fractures), hypercholesterolemia, and strokes with anastrozole and more muscle spasm, gynecological cancers and symptoms, vasomotor symptoms, and deep vein thromboses with tamoxifen.

In a second large RCT (NSABP B-35) of 3104 women with DCIS treated by lumpectomy with clear resection margins and whole breast irradiation, fewer recurrences or contralateral breast cancers were seen in women randomized to anastrozole. This benefit, however, was confined to women younger than 60 years of age. SF-12 physical and mental health component scale scores did not differ between treatment groups. As in the IBIS-II trial, side effects were common but differed as above between treatments.

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy alone has been considered for patients with triple-negative breast cancer (tests negative for estrogen receptors, progesterone receptors, and excess HER2 protein) and a pathological complete response (no cancer identified in the removed tissue). In one study of 328 women with triple-negative breast cancer who underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgical resection, chemotherapy did not eradicate the DCIS component in 55% and the presence of DCIS on core needle biopsy was associated with residual disease (OR 2.46, 95% CI 1.14-5.31).

In an international study of 166 women undergoing image-guided breast biopsy of a residual imaging abnormality or tumor bed after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, pathological response was highest among those with triple negative tumors (39/59, 66.1%) and lowest for hormone-receptor positive/HER2 negative tumors (5/31, 16%). Subgroup analysis of 76 women for whom a standardized protocol (i.e., image-guided vacuum-assisted biopsy of a tumor bed measuring <2 cm with 6 or more representative samples) was used allowed reliable prediction of residual disease with a false-negative rate of 3.2% and overall accuracy rate of 89.5% (95% CI 80.3%-95.3%).

Mastectomy with lymph node staging was the traditional approach to DCIS; reported combined local and distant recurrence rates are 1% to 2% with survival rates of 96% to 100%. It is considered the treatment of choice for DCIS with microinvasion and/or pleomorphic microcalcifications in more than one quadrant on mammography creating an area too large to excise with a cosmetically acceptable outcome.

The COMET study randomized 957 women with low risk DCIS (hormone receptor positive grade 1 or 2 without evidence of invasive cancer) tousual care (surgery +/- radiation) or active surveillance (mammography every 6 months for affected breast and every 12 months for unaffected breast). After 2 years there was no difference between groups in tumor size, invasive cancer (5.9% vs 4.2%) and mortality. Two other similar trials (LORIS and LORD) are underway.

Nipple-sparing mastectomy appears to be a reasonable approach with DCIS, invasive breast cancer or both based on a case series of 14 studies including 5980 women. In this study, overall 5-year survival ranged from 93% to 100%, 5-year local recurrence from 0% to 10%, locoregional recurrence 0% to 7.4%, and distant recurrence 1.6% to 15.6%.

Localized DCIS is usually treated with lumpectomy and follow-up radiation therapy. In 2 large RCTs with 10- to 12-year follow-up, women with localized DCIS randomized to receive lumpectomy without radiation had increased rates of subsequent recurrence of DCIS (26%-31% vs. 15%) and increased rates of subsequent invasive carcinoma (14%-17% vs. 7%-8%). One study found that women choosing mastectomy instead of breast-conserving surgery were younger and were more likely to have higher-grade tumors.

In an RCT of 298 patients with non-palpable invasive and in-situ breast cancers undergoing breast conserving surgery, there was no difference in recurrence at 5 years between those randomized to radioguided seed localization or wire localization of the tumor for resection. Recurrences occurred in 11 women (4%) at a median time of 26 months.

Pre-operative supine MRI with intraoperative optical scanning and tracking compared favorably with wire localization for positive margin rate in an RCT of women undergoing partial mastectomy for DCIS (N = 17), invasive breast cancer (N = 30) or both (N = 91). In this study, positive margins were observed in 68% and 58% of the cases underestimated by 2 cm or more using MRI and mammography, respectively, and in 15% and 14% of the cases not underestimated using MRI and mammography, respectively. Failure to obtain clear margins in patients undergoing mastectomy increases risk of local (HR 3.40, 95% CI 1.9-6.2) and distant (HR 1.53, 95% CI 1.03-2.25) recurrences among patients with breast cancer.

Consensus guidelines from the Society of Surgical Oncology, American Society for Radiation Oncology, and American Society of Clinical Oncology recommend a 2-mm margin as the standard for an adequate margin in DCIS treated with whole-breast irradiation.

In a population study using SEER cancer registry data, 56,053 women with DCIS had surgery and 1169 did not have surgery. Although the women who did not choose surgery were older and more likely to have low-grade disease, there was no survival difference after propensity weighting for women with low-grade lesions who had surgery vs. those who did not have surgery. There was, however, a difference for intermediate-grade and high-grade tumors favoring surgery.

A recent pooled analysis of 6 trials confirmed comparable effects on mortality for breast-conserving therapy (BCT) versus mastectomy for early breast cancer despite increased local and regional recurrence with BCT. It is not likely that there will be a randomized trial of these 2 therapies for DCIS.

SLNB does not appear necessary in DCIS but can be considered for large tumors (>2.5 cm), comedocarcinoma, or palpable mass. The NIH consensus statement concurs that for most women who have DCIS treated with excision, SLNB is not necessary.

SLNB may be considered at the time of mastectomy because there is approximately a 5% chance that invasive cancer will be found in the specimen and once a mastectomy has been performed, the opportunity is lost. Involvement of the axillary lymph node influences treatment decisions and prognosis, although the significance of a isolated tumor cells or micrometastases in a lymph node is unclear.
Risks of SLNB include lymphedema (about 3%), impaired shoulder movement (about 3%), arm or shoulder pain (about 8%), and numbness (about 12%).

Authors of a systematic review of 48 studies with 9,803 patients with DCIS who underwent SLNB found significant associations between tumor size >2 cm and high-grade DCIS with positive SNLB; SLNB be considered for these women.

In a meta-analysis of 4 large RCTs, adjuvant radiotherapy offered a significant reduction of invasive and DCIS ipsilateral breast cancer with odds ratios of 0.40 (95% CI 0.33-0.60) and 0.40 (95% CI 0.31-0.53), respectively. However, there were no differences in the likelihood of distant metastases or in death rates and there was a 1.53-fold increase in the likelihood of contralateral breast cancer in women in the radiotherapy arms. It remains unclear which patients may be candidates for excision alone.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 4 RCTs confirmed the benefit of radiation therapy (fewer ipsilateral breast events and ipsilateral recurrence) following breast-conserving surgery for DCIS. No long-term toxicity was found.

listitem.strong: Intraoperative radiotherapy vs. postoperative external beam radiotherapy

list.listitem: An RCT of 1113 women with invasive ductal carcinoma undergoing conservative surgery demonstrated single-dose targeted intraoperative radiotherapy was equivalent to external beam radiotherapy delivered over several weeks; at 4 years, there were similar recurrences (6 vs. 5, respectively). In a follow-up study of 146 women undergoing intraoperative radiation to the tumor bed for DCIS, 18% had acute complications including hematomas requiring drainage, infection treated with antibiotics, and erythema and 12% had chronic complications including a seroma, fibrosis and hyperpigmentation. This rate was lower than historical reports of complications following whole breast irradiation.

In another RCT with 2298 women aged 45 years and older with invasive ductal carcinoma up to 3.5 cm in size, cN0-N1, who were treated with lumpectomy, risk-adapted targeted intraoperative radiotherapy was comparable to external beam radiotherapy for overall survival (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.63-1.05), local recurrence-free survival (HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.91-1.41), and mastectomy-free survival (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.78-1.19).

listitem.strong: Whole breast vs. accelerated partial breast irradiation or dose adjustments

list.listitem: In a non-inferiority trial of 1184 patients with low-risk invasive and DCIS treated with breast-conserving surgery, there were no differences in local recurrence at 5 years between those randomized to either whole-breast irradiation or accelerated partial breast irradiation using multi-catheter brachytherapy (0.92% vs. 1.44%, respectively).

A similar result was demonstrated in a trial of 1065 women with DCIS or node-negative breast cancer treated by breast conserving surgery who were assigned to receive whole breast irradiation or twice daily accelerated partial breast irradiation. In this RCT, 8-year ipsilateral breast tumor recurrence rates were 2.8% vs. 3.0%, respectively. Although there was a higher rate of acute radiation toxicity in the whole breast irradiation group (45% vs. 28%) late radiation toxicity (13% vs. 32%) and adverse cosmesis (17.7% absolute difference at 7 years) was higher in the accelerated partial irradiation group, possibly due to the twice-daily regimen.

In an RCT of 1854 women with node-negative breast cancer or DCIS (N = 246) who underwent breast-conserving surgery and radiotherapy at a dose of either 50 Gy in 25 fr or 40 Gy in 15 fr, 9-year overall survival was comparable (93.4% for each study arm) as was 9-year locoregional recurrence (3.3% vs. 3.0%, respectively). There were no differences in cosmetic outcomes, patient satisfaction or radiation-associated cardiac and lung disease.

Among 1208 women with non-low-risk DCIS undergoing breast-conserving surgery and whole breast radiotherapy, those randomized to use of tumor bed boost following conventional whole breast radiotherapy or hypofractionated whole breast radiotherapy reported more persistent adverse effects on cosmetic status and arm and shoulder functional status.
DCIS is associated with high rates of long-term, disease-free survival (96%-98%) when treated with currently available therapies. B

In a follow-up of 1391 patients in a Hong Kong cancer registry aged ≥46 years with screen-detected DCIS of whom 372 were considered low risk based on nuclear grade, 10-year overall breast cancer-specific survival was (98.9%, 1136/1149), with no difference observed in low-risk vs. high-risk survival (99.5% vs. 98.6%).
The 5-year rate of recurrence of node-negative DCIS is between 9% and 30%. B

There is a higher risk of local recurrence and progression to invasive carcinoma with high-grade DCIS, the architectural pattern of comedo-necrosis, and the finding of microinvasive carcinoma associated with DCIS. DCIS that is extensive in distribution, is large in size, or involves the surgical resection margin also predicts a high likelihood for local recurrence. B In a meta-analysis of 18 studies, predictors of local invasive recurrence were positive margins and non-screening detected cancer.

Local recurrence rates for women with DCIS treated with mastectomy were 5.3% (27/508) for positive or close margins and 1.6% (37/2367) for negative margin based on 12 retrospective studies with a mean follow-up of 6.95 years; nearly all recurrences (93.7%) were invasive cancers. B

Investigators in Denmark found that many of the 574 women treated for DCIS suffered from pain (33%), sensory disturbances (about 33%), anxiety (20%) and depression (6%) and had unmet rehabilitation needs.

In the study from Hong Kong noted above, 46 (12.4%) patients in the low-risk group and 93 (12%) patients in the high-risk group did not receive surgery; the 10-year breast cancer-specific survival was 97.8% and 96.7%, respectively.

It is estimated that 25% to 40% of untreated DCIS will progress to invasive breast cancer. Predictors of invasive disease include lack of hormone receptor expression, DCIS lesions >15 mm, intermediate or high nuclear grade, and non-cribriform subtype of DCIS.

There is a higher risk of local recurrence and progression to invasive carcinoma with high-grade DCIS, the architectural pattern of comedo-necrosis, and the finding of microinvasive carcinoma associated with DCIS. DCIS that is extensive in distribution, is large in size, or involves the surgical resection margin also predicts a high likelihood for local recurrence. In a meta-analysis of 18 studies, predictors of local invasive recurrence were positive margins and non-screening detected cancer.
In women with DCIS not receiving RT, wider margins were associated with a lower rate of recurrence, based on one large retrospective study.

In one study of 415 patients with DCIS who underwent surgery, fourteen women (3.4%) had a recurrence at a median of 14 months. Predictors of recurrence based on preoperative MRI were greater functional tumor volume (median, 9.3 cm3 vs. 1.3 cm3), lesion peak signal enhancement ratio (median, 1.7 vs. 1.2) and background parenchymal enhancement volume (median, 58.3% vs. 41.1%) based on 11 women and 11 matched control women with no recurrence at a median of 102 months.

Immunostaining for topoisomerase IIIβ or CD10 expression may help predict distant metastasis and death (former) or relapse (latter). Topoisomerase IIIβ is a nuclear enzyme regulating DNA structure in eukaryotic cells and found in 33.9% of women with invasive ductal carcinoma in 1 study. CD10 is a myoepithelial cell surface peptidase found in normal levels in 29% of women with DCIS in 1 study.

listitem.strong: Health effects and quality of life

list.listitem: Investigators in Denmark found that many of the 574 women treated for DCIS suffered from pain (33%), sensory disturbances (about 33%), anxiety (20%) and depression (6%) and had unmet rehabilitation needs.

Women undergoing mastectomy and immediate breast reconstruction in one study had more negative body image and bodily pain but higher physical functioning than women post sector resection with or without radiation.

ACR (2019) recommends bilateral mammography (screening or diagnostic) or digital breast tomosynthesis (diagnostic or screening) as the most appropriate imaging modalities for surveillance for local recurrence following treatment for asymptomatic stage I breast cancer; MRI without and with contrast or US may be appropriate.

For patients who receive neoadjuvant chemotherapy, ACR suggests imaging with MRI without and with contrast in cases for which there is a prechemotherapy MRI, or US, diagnostic mammography or diagnostic digital breast tomosynthesis for evaluation of residual disease.
